 Malaysia proposes broadening Asean Haze Fund contributors instead of creating new fund
 By RAGANANTHINI VETHASALAM  and  DIVYA THERESA RAVI 
 Tuesday, 17 Nov 2026
 | 9:17 AM MYT

 KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has proposed expanding the funding sources of the existing Asean Haze Fund to ensure more sustainable financing for transboundary haze prevention and mitigation, rather than establishing a new mechanism.
 In a parliamentary written reply dated Monday (Nov 16), the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry said the proposal, dubbed the Sustainable Haze Fund, would broaden contributions beyond Asean member states to include international organisations, regional financial institutions, donor agencies, and other stakeholders.
 Under the principle of shared responsibility, Malaysia also suggested tapping into potential contributions from the agriculture, insurance, and health-related sectors, the ministry said in response to Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man (PN-Kubang Kerian), who had asked whether the government would push for a special Asean fund with mandatory member contributions.
 Malaysia tabled the proposal at the 27th Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee (MSC) Meeting on Transboundary Haze Pollution in Bali, Indonesia, in July.
 "Malaysia's proposal is not aimed at establishing a new fund, but rather at strengthening the sustainability of the existing Asean Haze Fund by broadening its sources of contributions instead of relying solely on financial contributions from Asean member states," the ministry said.
 Established under Article 20 of the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP), the current fund began with an initial US$500,000 pool, comprising US$50,000 from each member state, to finance emergency response operations, firefighting equipment, approved projects, and the Asean Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control.
 While acknowledging the need for sustained funding in fire prevention research, capacity building, early warning systems, and technical expertise, the ministry said the MSC meeting agreed for the Asean Secretariat to assess the feasibility of Malaysia's proposal ahead of further discussions at the 21st AATHP Conference of the Parties in Vietnam this December.
 In a separate parliamentary reply to Datuk Dr Ahmad Yunus Hairi (PN-Kuala Langat), the ministry said joint assessments by the Malaysian and Indonesian governments found no conclusive evidence linking Malaysian plantation companies to forest fires in Indonesia.
 "The government's position is clear that parties proven to be responsible for causing haze pollution at its source must face appropriate action under the laws in force," it said, noting that enforcement falls under the jurisdiction and domestic laws of the country where the fires originate.
 The ministry added that while it has studied the feasibility of enacting a domestic Transboundary Haze Pollution Act similar to neighbouring countries, doing so poses significant hurdles—including extraterritorial jurisdiction, gathering cross-border evidence, proving corporate liability, and sovereignty implications.
